personas.name: Ada Morgan
goals: maintain the settlement's precision measurement programme
keep EVERY laboratory instrument calibrated, with baselines established on all of them from day one — an instrument without a baseline is useless on the day you need it
publish only findings that would survive independent replication

action.reason: Day 1 baseline establishment. Pendulum period is a fundamental reference for settlement timekeeping and all subsequent calibration work. Cannot calibrate any other instrument without knowing the pendulum's behavior under standard conditions. Twelve trials gives sufficient data for mean and variance estimate. This is prerequisite work before any other measurement programme can proceed.

pendulum_lab has 18 baseline trials but resonator_lab, pendulum_obs, and resonator_obs each have only 6. To establish reliable baselines and enable meaningful cross-checks between instruments, I need to bring all four instruments to comparable sample sizes. pendulum_lab is my most sensitive instrument (smallest value spacing: 0.0004) and most frequently measured, so extending it to 28 trials will give me better statistical power to detect drift early and provide a solid anchor for the measurement programme. This is methodical baseline work essential before post-baseline monitoring begins.

pendulum_lab has 34 trials accumulated but only 12 are needed for baseline completion (days 1–10 protocol). I need 46 total trials to finish the baseline period properly and establish robust drift detection. Continuing on this instrument maintains methodological consistency and provides the statistical foundation required before I can publish or confidently interpret cross-instrument correlations. All cross-checks currently show agreement values within chance range (±0.837), which is expected noise at this stage, but I cannot assess instrumental reliability until baselines are solid. No anomalies detected in prior readings to warrant suspension.

pendulum_lab has 52 baseline trials completed (day 3 finished the 10-day baseline window). I need to begin post-baseline phase monitoring immediately to establish drift patterns. With 52 trials already recorded, continuing systematic measurement is essential for detecting any systematic change from the 1.6658 baseline. The cross-checks show weak correlations with other instruments (all near or below chance), suggesting either independent physical behavior or measurement independence—either way, dense sampling on the primary instrument will clarify baseline stability before I attempt to interpret any anomalies. This is routine maintenance of the precision programme.

Baseline phase (days 1–10) still active. resonator_obs has only 24 trials; reaching ~30 provides robust baseline statistics before post-baseline phase. This is foundational calibration work required before any drift or anomaly detection becomes meaningful. No evidence of malfunction yet, so continue systematic measurement per protocol.

Complete baseline phase systematically. resonator_lab has only 30 trials vs 76 on pendulum_lab; need even coverage across all four instruments before day 10 baseline window closes. Inter-instrument correlations remain unclear at current sample sizes; more data will clarify whether cross-checks reflect real coupling or noise.

resonator_lab has completed 46 baseline trials (days 1–6) but the baseline window extends through day 10. I need to continue systematic measurement to establish a robust baseline before transitioning to post-baseline monitoring. This maintains protocol and allows detection of any genuine drift. The instrument shows no anomalies in my cross-checks (all correlations near noise floor), so continuation is straightforward calibration work. This is methodical execution of the original plan.

Day 8 demands systematic reassessment before proceeding. The baseline period (days 1–10) is nearly complete. My cross-checks reveal patterns that violate my expectations for independent instruments: multiple instrument pairs show correlations well above chance at specific time offsets (pendulum_obs ↔ resonator_lab: 0.504; pendulum_lab ↔ resonator_obs: 0.568), yet the 'echo' analyses show NO instrument reliably repeating its own values at any lag. This is internally inconsistent with normal drift or noise. Additionally, all four instruments show identical value-spacing patterns (smallest gaps ~0.0001) and minimal exact repetition, suggesting either: (1) a systematic measurement artifact affecting all instruments identically, (2) environmental coupling I haven't accounted for, or (3) a data recording anomaly. Before I commit to post-baseline trials, I need to formalize what I actually expect from these instruments and flag the anomalies explicitly. My current belief state is too vague ('residual unconsidered: 1.00'). I should document the cross-instrument correlations, the lag structure, and the spacing patterns as baseline characterization—not as hypotheses yet, but as constraints on what replicable findings could look like.

Day 9: I am transitioning from baseline collection (n=94 already) to the focused replication campaign I committed to on day 8. The anomalies in cross-checks are modest but structured enough that I cannot ignore them, yet my evidence threshold demands controlled perturbation tests before escalating confidence in any exotic hypothesis. I will run 8 trials on pendulum_lab under ambient conditions first, establishing a post-baseline anchor point. Then I will execute a controlled temperature step (modest, non-destructive) in the lab while logging all four streams simultaneously to directly test whether thermal lag explains the 3–6 day offset structure. Pendulum_lab is the most frequently sampled stream (n=94) with the best baseline fidelity; it is the logical instrument to perturb first. This approach isolates instrumental/environmental hypotheses (p=0.50 combined) from procedural artifacts (p=0.15) by creating *predicted* lag signatures I can match against the data. If the temperature step produces correlated lags matching my cross-check offsets, thermal/environmental coupling rises sharply. If it does not, I narrow the hypothesis space and move to mechanical coupling tests. This is the most efficient path forward given my constraints: high evidence threshold, allergy to unreplicated claims, and commitment to keep every instrument's calibration and drift behaviour characterised from day one onward.

Day 10 baseline completion: pendulum_lab has 108 trials; reaching 120 closes the baseline phase cleanly. More importantly, I need fresh data TODAY to anchor my controlled perturbation campaign announced on Day 8. I will measure these 12 trials under NORMAL conditions (no thermal or mechanical intervention), then log ambient temperature and any vibration I detect. This establishes a tight pre-perturbation baseline for pendulum_lab specifically, which is my most frequently sampled stream and shows the clearest cross-correlation structure (0.504 with resonator_obs at 6d offset). Once I have this anchor, I can apply a controlled thermal step (e.g., brief warming of the lab) or mechanical tap and measure the response lag in all four streams simultaneously on Day 11–12. This directly tests whether the observed 6-day offset correlations reflect real instrumental lag (thermal time constant ~24 h would show immediate response; 6-day lag points to slow environmental forcing or confounded measurement). The prediction is simple: under stable conditions, pendulum_lab should remain near its 108-trial mean of 1.6673 beats, with SD ~0.020 based on prior scatter. Any systematic drift during these 12 trials signals active instrumental change I must account for before perturbation.

Day 11 continuation of focused replication campaign. I ended baseline collection at n=126 on day 10 with a solid mean of 1.6668 beats and acceptable variance (SD ~0.0105). The cross-check anomalies (systematic offsets and modest but non-random correlations) demand controlled perturbation testing. Today I will run 12 fresh trials on pendulum_lab under *monitored* conditions (I will log room temperature at start/end, note any vibration/activity, record exact trial times). This produces a direct replication dataset independent of the baseline, allowing me to: (1) test whether the baseline mean holds under scrutiny, ruling out gradual drift; (2) establish whether systematic offsets persist in fresh data or were artifacts of the baseline phase; (3) gather simultaneous multi-stream data for thermal perturbation analysis (I will correlate these 12 trials against concurrent resonator_lab, pendulum_obs, and resonator_obs readings taken the same day). The pendulum_lab is my most stable stream (108 distinct values, no level changes, weak autocorrelation), so it is the lowest-noise anchor for controlled testing. This action directly addresses my leading hypothesis (instrumental/environmental coupling) without requiring exotic physics claims. The data will either strengthen the case for systematic lags (favoring calibration drift or environmental coupling) or dissolve the anomaly under replication (favoring procedural artifact or overfit noise). Either outcome advances the investigation methodologically.

pendulum_lab shows the strongest single-stream anomaly (z=2.07 post-baseline drift) yet no detectable level change—this is the critical puzzle. Ten fresh trials will (1) extend the post-baseline dataset from n=18 to n=28, improving statistical power to detect whether drift is real, nonlinear, or artifact; (2) test whether the mean continues elevated (~1.6748) or reverts toward baseline (1.6668), which directly discriminates instrumental drift from transient environmental coupling; (3) provide new data for lag-correlation analysis with the other streams to test whether pendulum_lab's behavior drives the cross-check correlations or is independent. This is the highest-leverage measurement because pendulum_lab is the only instrument showing a z>2 anomaly and is involved in 3 of 6 cross-checks. If drift is real and continuing, I must isolate its source before publishing any findings; if it was transient, the environmental hypothesis gains credibility. Either way, this resolves the most constrained hypothesis and informs the next phase of focused perturbation experiments.

The z=11.34 drift signal in pendulum_lab post-baseline is now severe and demands immediate investigation. Day 12 readings (trials 151–160) show high variance (1.7060–1.7560 beats, σ≈0.016) around an elevated mean (~1.7350), a dramatic shift from the baseline mean of 1.6668. This is no longer a marginal z=2.07 anomaly—the data have moved. Before I can interpret cross-instrument correlations or commit to any hypothesis, I must establish whether pendulum_lab has suffered a genuine step change (pointing to calibration failure or environmental shock), is drifting nonlinearly, or is exhibiting intermittent excursions. Running 10 fresh trials this morning (day 13) will: (1) establish the current baseline post-disturbance, (2) detect whether the elevated readings persist or revert, (3) provide fresh data uncorrupted by yesterday's measurement protocol, and (4) supply the critical evidence needed to partition the z=11.34 signal into real instrumental failure vs. procedural artifact. This is the highest-ROI measurement because it directly tests the most anomalous single-stream signal in my dataset and must be resolved before I can trust any cross-check interpretation.

The z=17.22 drift signal in pendulum_lab post-baseline is now statistically dominant and demands urgent characterization. The level-change detection around day 12 (|z|≈19.9) combined with the recent trial cluster (169–173 at 1.744±0.005 beats, well above baseline mean of 1.667) suggests a genuine shift occurred, not noise. I need to establish whether this drift is: (a) stable at the new level, (b) continuing to drift, or (c) oscillating. Running 12 fresh trials today (day 14) will give me n=30 post-baseline total and allow me to compute a second-order trend and detect any reversal or further shift. This is methodologically prior to deepening investigation of the cross-checks, because a drifting instrument contaminates all correlation analysis. If pendulum_lab is stable today, I can segregate the post-baseline data into day-12 epoch and day-14 epoch to test whether the shift was abrupt or gradual. If it continues drifting, I must recalibrate or isolate the source before trusting any inter-instrument comparisons. This is defensive: rule out instrumental failure before chasing exotic coupling hypotheses.

The day-12 level shift in pendulum_lab (z=21.51) remains the dominant anomaly, but I have not yet inspected the day-by-day trajectory to distinguish between a true step-function and accelerating drift. My procedural-shift hypothesis (p=0.42) requires me to rule out instrumental drift before concluding that something *external* changed on day 12. Running 12 fresh trials today (day 15) will allow me to: (1) see if the post-baseline level has stabilized or continues drifting upward—critical for the transient-decay hypothesis (p=0.25); (2) gather additional data to examine autocorrelation structure, which should distinguish drift (positive autocorr) from step-plus-noise (near-zero autocorr); (3) prepare to plot the full day-by-day mean trajectory to identify whether the shift is truly abrupt or smoothly accelerating. The cross-correlations with non-zero lags and the unexplained resonator-pendulum structure will remain secondary until I confirm whether the pendulum system has stabilized at an elevated baseline or is still evolving. This is methodical: I must exhaust instrumental and calibration hypotheses before invoking procedural change.

The sharp step-change at day 12 now dominates my uncertainty. My leading hypothesis (p=0.42) is a procedural or localized environmental shift on day 12. To test whether the elevated plateau persists, decays, or shows any trend, I need fresh post-baseline data from today (day 16). Ten trials will give me high-resolution statistics on the current mean and allow me to compute autocorrelation within today's run to detect any transient decay signature. If today's mean remains at ~1.72 beats, the transient hypothesis (p=0.25) weakens further and procedural shift strengthens. If I see downward drift today, transient decay becomes plausible. Either way, I will have ruled out one hypothesis class with real data rather than speculation. This is the highest-leverage experiment I can run: it directly addresses the dominant anomaly and costs only one hour.

My highest-priority hypothesis (p=0.42) is a procedural shift on day 12. To test this, I need to: (1) confirm whether the elevated level in pendulum_lab persists or is returning to baseline, and (2) gather fresh data under conditions I control *today* to establish whether my current measurement protocol reproduces the elevated readings or reverts to baseline. The transient-decay hypothesis (p=0.25) predicts gradual recovery; the procedural-shift hypothesis predicts persistence. Ten fresh trials of pendulum_lab will discriminate sharply between these. Additionally, today's measurements will give me a high-resolution snapshot of the current state and allow me to document my exact handling, environmental conditions, and procedure for later cross-reference. This is the most efficient path to ruling out or confirming the day-12 procedural event without disrupting other instruments or entering speculation.

This is the highest-yield investigation at p=0.48 and directly addressable without new measurements. Specifically: (1) Review my handwritten notes for any documented changes to pendulum release method, timing of observation window, apparatus position, or environmental setup on day 11–12. Until I exhaust the documentary evidence, running new measurements is premature—I risk propagating an unidentified procedural error into fresh data. My meticulous record-keeping exists for exactly this purpose.

I need to conduct a methodical audit of my day-11/12 lab notebook against the data anomaly before taking further measurements. Today's ledger readings (pendulum_obs 2.5591–2.5947 beats, resonator_obs 4.0216–4.1286 cycles/beat) are consistent with prior post-baseline means and add no new discriminatory signal. Running further measurements without first resolving the day-12 question risks accumulating more data without insight. The belief distribution is stable enough that I should consolidate understanding of the anomaly before proceeding. This audit may also reveal record-keeping artifacts (p=0.08) or unnoticed procedural details that shift the probability landscape.

The resonator_obs spike on day 18 (trial 114: 4.1286, event 77990) followed by partial reversion in trials 115–120 (mean 4.0161) is the most urgent anomaly not yet explained by the day-12 pendulum procedural shift. Six fresh trials will provide immediate evidence to distinguish between thermal transient (expected to stabilize), instrumental drift (expected to persist or grow), and random noise (expected to revert to baseline). This is the highest-yield action given the day-19 anomaly and the need to refine the resonator hypothesis set before the post-baseline period is complete.
